$comment: A corpus of stale-selector failures, so a change to healing reports a number
instead of an opinion. Each case is a page, a selector that no longer resolves
against it, and the element the test actually meant.
Run by tests/unit/corpus.test.js. It measures two things offline, with no model
reachable  - the intended element is in the candidate list, addressed by a
locator that resolves to exactly one element on the live page.
This is the precondition for any heal: when it fails, no model
can succeed no matter how well it reasons.
engine     - given a model answer, the engine heals to the intended element.
`expect.free` marks a case no candidate can cover — an element with no accessible
name — where the model is expected to fall back to writing a locator. Those cases
assert reachability is *absent*, which is what keeps the fallback path honest.
Add a case whenever a real heal fails. The first one below is transcribed from a
healing record, which is why it is first.

cases.name: nav item renamed and moved, with one plausible successor
cases.note: The decidable form of the case from the real healing record. Only one navigation item could have been 'Charter Cloud' — the others are plainly unrelated — so the rename can be inferred from the page alone. A model should heal this.

cases.name: nav item renamed, two equally plausible successors — must NOT guess
cases.note: The form the real record actually had: 'Charter Cloud' is gone and both 'Private Cloud' and 'Dedicated Cloud' could be its successor. Nothing on the page decides between them — the original gpt-4o answer picked one, which was a coin flip. The correct outcome is a refusal, and claude-haiku-4-5 refused three runs out of three with reasoning like 'without knowing which should replace it, I cannot safely map the old selector'. Healing here would be the 'wrong element that works' failure. Only history — the page as it was — could make this decidable.

cases.name: two links share a name, so the answer must be scoped
cases.note: Ambiguity is the other half of the problem: a name that is not unique has no flat locator at all, and offering one that matches two elements would only move the failure to strict mode.

cases.name: one name is a prefix of another
cases.note: getByRole matches a name as a substring by default, so an unqualified { name: 'Submit' } matches three buttons here. Every candidate sets exact: true for this reason.

cases.name: moved into a dialog, same name
icon button with no accessible name
cases.note: Nothing names this element and the accessibility snapshot carries no test ids, so the model used to guess a locator — about half the time. It is now offered by its test id, and the locator is written by this package.
cases.description: the close button in the corner

cases.name: table row action, addressed through its row

expect.name: Edit
expect.selector: getByRole('row', { name: 'Gadget Edit' }).getByRole('button', { name: 'Edit', exact: true })

cases.note: Two buttons named Edit, one per row. Only the row tells them apart, so the expectation must name the row: an unscoped { role: 'button', name: 'Edit' } matches both, and for a while this case silently checked the Widget row's button while claiming to check Gadget's.

cases.name: clickable list item that nothing names
cases.note:
From a healing record (v0.4.5). A menu built as
  • Charter Cloud
    • with a click handler: listitem takes no accessible name from its contents and the span has no role, so nothing is addressable by role. The model answered getByText('Charter Cloud', { exact: true }) — correct — and the intent check refused it because the model had described the element as a listitem while its selector landed on the text node inside. The stale selector keeps the /a: the redesign removed the anchor, so the test's path no longer exists. An earlier version used //li/span, which matches this page and so was never stale — it measured the healer rewriting a working selector.

cases.name: same menu with the anchor still present
cases.note: The likelier shape of the page above: the test removed the /a from its own XPath to force a miss, so the anchor is still there and the item IS addressable by role. The role candidate is the durable one and must be preferred over the text handle.
